newsitem.title: UK: Austria raises cheaper funds via guilder Eurobond.
newsitem.headline: Austria raises cheaper funds via guilder Eurobond.

text.p: Austria raised 1.0 billion guilders ($505 million) on the international bond markets on Wednesday, borrowing the 30-year funds more cheaply than it could at home, bankers said.

The jumbo guilder Eurobond will transform into an existing 30-year domestic Austrian government bond if it joins monetary union. If the Netherlands adopts a European currency, Austria can choose to redenominate the bond into euros.
"There is a huge pocket of demand for guilders among Dutch investors and they are very hungry for sovereign assets," an official at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, lead manager of the deal, said.
"This bond is very much tapping into a different investor base to the domestic 30-year deal, and Austria was able to raise funds slightly more cheaply than it could at home," he said.
Wednesday's guilder bond pays a 6.25 percent coupon and matures on July 15, 2027, terms which are identical to those on Austria's 30-year Bunds launched on Tuesday.
Both transactions can be stripped, which means the coupon payments can be separated from the principal.
The guilder bond offers investors 14 basis points over the long-dated Dutch state loan.
"Austria is a fantastic name in the guilder market and has not been seen for about a 1.5 years," the ABN AMRO official said.
"There was pent-up demand for both the name and the maturity. That helped us to price the deal at 14 over, which is really quite tight," he said.
Nearly the whole guilder deal sold out on Wednesday, with around 70 percent placed with Dutch institutions and the rest bought by Italian, British and German funds.
But Austria's 15 billion schillings ($1.2 billion) 30-year Bunds met with weaker demand from domestic investors, bankers said.

Vienna traders on Tuesday said the timing of the long-dated bonds were good from Austria's point of view because they were able to tap into historically low interest rates, but Austrian investors were hesitant to take on the rate risk for 30 years.
They said international investors had more experience with such long maturities, but domestic Austrian buyers were more cautious.

In January Austria became the first borrower to launch a Eurobond which would redenominate into euros after EMU, with a 5.0 billion French franc ($842 million) bond. A host of other borrowers, including European sovereigns, companies and banks, have since issued similar transactions.
-- Aline van Duyn, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7748 ($ = 1.981 Dutch Guilders) ($ = 12.38 Austrian Schillings) ($ = 5.936 French Francs)
